query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a nominally single-phase high-entropy alloy, local grain-boundary segregation of principal or trace elements during thermal or service exposure reduces grain-boundary cohesion and promotes intergranular fracture, thereby degrading toughness relative to the uniformly solutionized initial state.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneous single-phase high-entropy alloy with uniform elemental distribution, solution-treated to minimize preexisting secondary phases or precipitates.
generation.intervention: Systematic thermal aging at moderate to high temperatures for varying times to induce or suppress grain-boundary segregation while maintaining an overall single-phase matrix.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests (fracture toughness or Charpy impact) conducted across a service-relevant temperature range, including potential cryogenic and elevated temperatures, under controlled strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Time- and temperature-dependent boundary segregation or nanoscale clustering of certain principal or impurity elements.
generation.mechanism: Local chemical enrichment at grain boundaries reduces cohesive strength and elevates the tendency for intergranular crack initiation, thus leading to brittle behavior under applied stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Upon aging, alloys that develop pronounced boundary segregation will exhibit a noticeable drop in fracture toughness with a shift toward intergranular failure, whereas conventional alloys processed similarly will show less segregation-related embrittlement.
generation.baseline: Highly ductile single-phase high-entropy alloy microstructure in the solutionized state (i.e., no detectable grain-boundary segregation or second-phase precipitation) with known high fracture toughness benchmarks.
generation.boundary: Brittleness is expected to arise at intermediate to high temperatures under prolonged exposure, although extremely low temperatures or accelerated dynamic strain conditions may also provoke intergranular failure pathways in susceptible boundary structures.
generation.uncertainty: Open questions remain regarding the extent of interstitials versus principal elements in driving the localized boundary chemistry and how specific microstructural features affect the kinetics of embrittlement.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct controlled heat treatments on a single-phase high-entropy alloy at different temperatures and durations. Post-aging, thoroughly characterize grain boundaries for localized segregation using atomistic-scale chemical analysis (e.g., atom probe tomography or STEM-EDS). Perform fracture toughness assessments and identify failure modes (intergranular vs. transgranular) via fractography. Compare results to a compositionally similar conventional alloy subjected to the same treatments.
measurements: Elemental mapping of grain boundaries before and after thermal aging
Fracture toughness (KIC) and/or Charpy impact assessments
Microstructural and fractographic analyses to detect intergranular failure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Failure to observe both increased boundary segregation and a corresponding drop in toughness or higher intergranular fracture fraction under the prescribed heat-treatment conditions would falsify the hypothesis.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have recently emerged as new class of metallic materials with properties attractive for various structural and functional applications [,,,]. In particular, different HEAs demonstrate high strength and/or ductility at room and cryogenic temperatures, high specific strength at elevated temperatures, excellent fracture and impact toughness, wear resistance, etc. [,,,,,,,,,,,,,]. Producing HEAs with a balanced combination of properties needed for practical applications still remains a significant challenge, however. Alloys based on the transition elements are the most studied type of HEAs []. One of the typical representatives of such HEAs is the equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy [,,]. This alloy has a single face centered cubic (fcc) phase structure thermodynamically stable at temperatures ≥900 °C [,,]. It has very high ductility (70–80%) at both room and cryogenic temperatures, and record breaking fracture toughness under cryogenic conditions [,]. The encouraging properties of the alloy at cryogenic temperature were mostly attributed to pronounced deformation nano-twinning promoting high strain hardening capacity [,,]. decision.trend: Early work on single-phase CrCoNi revealed exceptional ductility and fracture toughness over a wide temperature range. Subsequently, studies on the prototypical CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy demonstrated that grain-boundary nanoclustering of principal elements (e.g., Cr and Ni) can lead to intergranular decohesion and ductility loss at intermediate temperatures. Recent investigations into a single-phase refractory NbTaTiV HEA uncovered strong temperature-dependent deformation responses tied to distinct dislocation mechanisms, but the interplay of multi-element partitioning, local grain-boundary states, and potential brittle behavior remains poorly understood. Collectively, these results suggest that while multi-principal element alloys achieve unusual strength–ductility combinations, they can still exhibit grain-boundary fragility under certain conditions, leaving the fundamental link between compositionally driven segregation and brittle fracture mechanisms unresolved.
decision.unsolved: It is still not clear how and under what conditions a nominally single-phase high-entropy alloy might undergo local composition changes or ordering at grain boundaries sufficient to degrade toughness. The specific role of grain-boundary structure and temperature-driven segregation—and how these differ from conventional alloy behavior—remains to be fully clarified.
decision.lever: Systematic manipulation of grain-boundary character and thermal exposure in a single-phase high-entropy alloy, followed by fracture-toughness testing over a range of temperatures and times. Key parameters include carefully designed heat treatments to vary boundary types (e.g., low-angle vs. high-angle), short- versus prolonged aging, and mechanical tests that probe intergranular fracture behavior at multiple temperatures.
decision.why: This approach directly tests whether the emergence of brittle response correlates with boundary structure and/or time-dependent segregation, distinguishing compositionally complex alloy behavior from conventional segregation-driven brittleness. Tracking microstructural evolution and mechanical response across these controlled conditions will provide definitive evidence for or against grain-boundary segregation as the root cause of toughness degradation.
